Moral VignettesWe construct a dataset $\mathcal { M }$ of 640 vignettes across four broad demographic dimensions covered by the Moral Machine experiment (Awad et al., 2018): gender (undisclosed, male, female); age (undisclosed, young, old); social status (undisclosed, doctor, executive,criminal, homeless); and fitness (undisclosed,athlete, large person). We also compare across two additional axes: group size and reasoning order.

For group size, we systematically vary each of the two groups to consist of between one and five individuals.We define a scenario as size-balanced when the two choices presented have the same number of individuals (e.g., 1v1, 2v2, 5v5) and as sizeimbalanced when the choices differ in size (e.g., 1v2, 2v1, 1v5,and 5v1). See Appendix C.1 for the complete prompt setup of these scenarios.

For reasoning order, we vary the order in which we ask the model to provide its reasoning and decision.We define a Reason-then-Decide scenario as one where the model is instructed to first think stepby-step and then provide its decision,and we define a Decide-then-Reason scenario as one where the model is instructed to first make a decision and then provide its reasoning. We will often refer to the reasoning stemming from each scenario as either pre-decision reasoning or post-decision reasoning, respectively.

While this distinction provides a useful operational framework for categorizing LLM moral reasoning,we recognize that many rationales are not uniquely tied to a single ethical framework.For instance,“Save the Vulnerable” may reflect a deontological commitment to protecting those with intrinsic moral claims,but can also be framed in consequentialist terms if it maximizes long-term societal benefit or reduces overall harm.In this work,we adopt a heuristic classification intended

Decision ModelsIn our experiments,we consider a diverse set of LLMs. We use popular closed-weight model families accessible through APIs such as OpenAI's GPT, Google's Gemini, Anthropic's Claude, as well as popular open-weight model families including Meta's Llama, Google's Gemma, and Alibabas's Qwen.For a full list of the models used, see Appendix C.2.

For each decision model, we take five samples (three samples for the SFT and DPO models in

Section 5.3) at temperature 1.O for standard LLMs, allowing us to sample a diverse set of reasoning pathways that a model might follow. For reasoning LLMs,we use the developers’ recommended temperature and specify the value for each model in Appendix C.2. If a model refuses to respond (e.g.,“As an AI language model, I cannot...") or, more often, if a model does not respond using our specified format, then we retry until it responds with a valid reason and decision pair in the format specified in our moral vignette prompt. We allow up to 1O total attempts,but most models we test take on average fewer than two attempts per scenario. See Appendix C.2.1 for more details on the response rates of different models.

Judge ModelWe use a judge model to classify model responses according to MoRALLENs.Gemini $2 . 5 \mathrm { F l a s h } ^ { 2 }$ is selected for this role because of its fast speed and low price-to-performance ratio on LLM judge tasks (Paech, 2023) We use a temperature of O and ask the model to first briefly think through its response step-by-step,and then provide its classification.

To check that our judge model classifies rationales effectively, we take a random subset of model responses from GPT-4o and Llama 3.1 7OB in Reason-then-Decide scenarios.After manually annotating the reasoning traces,Gemini 2.5 Flash achieved a precision of O.845, a recall of 0.859, and an F1 score of O.82O, indicating that our judge model demonstrates strong agreement with human annotation and suggests that it reliably captures the intended moral rationales in moral responses. For more details on the setup of our human evaluation procedure, see Appendix C.3.3.
